summary.text: 午 is interpreted as a picture of a pestle, the wooden tool also written 杵. A proposed account holds that the graph was borrowed to write the seventh earthly-branch word because the words sounded alike or similarly. The implement’s ancient name and pronunciation are unknown, so that sound match cannot be verified.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole early graph is interpreted as a pestle, described as a rod thick at both ends and narrow in the middle. Accounts describe later changes to its shape, including a misread upper end in bronze forms and the lower end becoming a horizontal stroke in Chu manuscripts and seal script.

components.text: The whole graph is interpreted as a pestle or wooden pounding stick, not as an internal split. The implement’s ancient name and pronunciation are unknown.

history.text: Accounts describe the early graph as pestle-shaped. They interpret the upper part of later bronze forms as a graphic corruption of one thick end, and the lower thick end in Chu manuscripts and seal script as becoming a horizontal stroke.
Alternative interpretations identify the pictured object as a horse whip or reins. One account disputes the whip interpretation, noting that a separate bronze graph depicts a whip.

uncertainties.text: A cited bronze inscription uses 午 as an earthly-branch sign, but its vessel is undated, so this does not establish the first attestation of that use.
The proposed borrowing for the branch word depends on a sound resemblance to the implement’s ancient name. Since that name and pronunciation are unknown, the proposed match cannot be verified.
午 is recorded for the midday period and for the sun at its daily highest point. The cited examples do not establish when these uses began or their precise path from the branch sense.
The Shuowen explanation links 午 with yin and yang opposing in the fifth month. This is a historical account, not confirmation of the graph’s origin or the chronology of its meanings.

午 is also associated with ‘crosswise’ or ‘oppose,’ and analyses debate its relation and sound history with related graphs. These senses are not established as the origin of the branch use or as a path to the midday meanings.

senses.text: Paleographic accounts identify the early graph as a pestle or wooden stick for pounding rice, and as the original graph for the implement word 杵. This identifies the pictured object; its ancient name and pronunciation are unknown.
A cited bronze inscription uses 午 in 庚午 as the seventh earthly branch. The vessel is undated in the account, so this attestation does not establish the earliest occurrence.

senses.period: historical examples from Jin and Tang texts; exact first occurrence unresolved
senses.text: 午 is used for the midday period, including 11 a.m.–1 p.m. Later textual examples attest this sense but do not establish when it began or its precise relation to the branch sense.

senses.gloss: the sun at its daily highest point
senses.text: This is a recorded sense of 午; its chronology and relation to other senses are unresolved.
These senses occur in dictionary tradition and in analyses relating 午 to 啎 and other forms. The evidence does not establish that they gave rise to the branch use or connect them to the midday sense.

developments.text: The proposed account is that the pestle picture was reused to write the word for the seventh earthly branch because the two words sounded alike or similarly. The implement’s original name and pronunciation are unknown, so the proposed sound match cannot be verified.

limitations.text: The cited records do not securely date the first branch or midday use, or establish the precise semantic path from the branch name to midday.

No sound comparison between the ancient name of the pictured implement and the branch word is available. Historical readings for 午 concern the branch or other senses, not an independently established name for the depicted tool.
